about: Exam-only questions for the two fixed practice exams (docs/apprecalc-architecture.md, "Practice exams"): four-option calculator questions for Section I Part B, ids pcalc-exam-<form>-<nn>, with their stimuli (exam-<form>-s<n>). Every key is recomputed in EXAM_NUMBERS (scripts/lib/apprecalc-exams.mjs).

exam-1-s1.title: Visitors to a pop-up museum
exam-1-s1.text: A pop-up museum counted its visitors each week. Use a graphing calculator, and store each regression with all its digits.

table.caption: Number of visitors V during week x after a pop-up museum opened

exam-2-s1.title: Depth of a reservoir
exam-2-s1.text: The depth of the water in a reservoir is modeled by $w(t) = -0.02t^3 + 0.5t^2 - 2t + 30$ meters, $t$ months after the start of a year, for $0 \le t \le 20$. Use a graphing calculator.

plot.label: Graph of w(t) = -0.02t cubed + 0.5t squared - 2t + 30 for t from 0 to 20 months: it dips slightly to about 27.8 near t = 2.3, rises to about 45.2 near t = 14.3, then falls back to 30 at t = 20

exam-2-s2.title: Hours of daylight
exam-2-s2.text: The number of hours of daylight in a city is modeled by $D(t) = 12.2 + 2.8\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{365}(t - 80)\right)$, $t$ days after January 1, for $0 \le t \le 365$. Use a graphing calculator in radian mode.

plot.label: Graph of D(t) = 12.2 + 2.8 sin(2 pi (t - 80) / 365) for t from 0 to 365 days: one full wave between 9.4 and 15 hours, crossing the midline 12.2 going up at t = 80

items.q: Let $p(x) = -0.5x^3 + 3x^2 - 2x + 1$. What is the relative maximum value of $p$ on the interval $0 < x < 6$?

why.correct: Graph $p$ in a window such as $0 \le x \le 6$ by $-12 \le y \le 12$ and use the calculator's maximum feature. The high point between the two turning points is at $x \approx 3.633$, where $p(x) \approx 9.355$. Evaluate $p$ at the stored $x$-value rather than at a rounded one.
options: Right: the greatest output near the turning point at $x \approx 3.633$, where $p$ changes from increasing to decreasing.
This is the input where the relative maximum occurs; the question asks for the value of $p$ there.
This is the relative minimum value, at $x \approx 0.367$, where $p$ changes from decreasing to increasing.
This is $p(0)$, the value at the left end of the interval, which is lower than the high point.

items.q: Use a graphing calculator to find every real zero of $f(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 3$.

why.correct: A cubic has at most three real zeros. Graph $f$ in a window that shows both turning points and both ends, such as $-2 \le x \le 5$, and use the zero feature for each $x$-intercept: $x \approx -0.700$, $x \approx 1.239$ and $x \approx 3.461$.
options: Right: all three $x$-intercepts of the graph, each correct to three decimal places.
This misses the negative zero; a window starting at $x = 0$ hides the crossing near $x = -0.7$.
These are the zeros of $f(-x)$: every sign is flipped, as if the graph were reflected across the $y$-axis.
These are the inputs of the two turning points, where $f$ changes direction, not where $f(x) = 0$.

items.q: Use quadratic regression to model the data as $V(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. What is $a$, correct to three decimal places?

why.correct: Enter the weeks and the visitor counts as two lists and run a quadratic regression: $a \approx -3.429$, $b \approx 29.714$ and $c \approx 15.429$. Store the regression in the calculator for the next questions. The negative $a$ fits counts that rise and then fall.
options: Right: the coefficient of $x^2$ in the quadratic regression.
This is $b$, the coefficient of $x$, not the coefficient of $x^2$.
This is $c$, the constant term of the regression.
This is the slope of a linear regression on the same data, a different model.

items.q: Using the stored quadratic regression $V$, how many visitors does the model predict for week $x = 8$?

why.correct: Evaluate the stored model: $V(8) \approx 33.714$ visitors. Use the stored coefficients, not rounded ones. Week 8 is past the last data point, so the prediction is less certain than one inside the data.
options: This is the linear regression at $x = 8$; a line keeps rising, but the counts rise and then fall.
This uses the coefficients rounded to three decimal places first; rounding partway changes the answer.
Right: the stored quadratic regression evaluated at $x = 8$.
This is the model at $x = 7$, the last week in the table, not week 8.

items.q: Using the stored regression $V$, what is the average rate of change of $V$ on $[1, 5]$, in visitors per week?

why.correct: The average rate of change of $V$ on $[1, 5]$ is $\frac{V(5) - V(1)}{5 - 1} \approx \frac{36.571}{4} \approx 9.143$ visitors per week, the slope of the secant line through $(1, V(1))$ and $(5, V(5))$ on the model's graph.
options: This is the change $V(5) - V(1)$, not divided by the $4$ weeks.
This uses the table values $42$ and $78$; the question asks about the model $V$.
This subtracts in the wrong order: $V(1) - V(5)$ over $5 - 1$.
Right: the slope of the secant line of the model on $[1, 5]$.

items.q: A town had $1{,}200$ residents at $t = 0$ and $1{,}950$ residents at $t = 6$, with $t$ in years. An exponential model $P(t) = ab^t$ passes through both points. What is $b$, correct to three decimal places?

why.correct: $a = 1{,}200$, so $1{,}200b^6 = 1{,}950$ and $b^6 = 1.625$. Then $b = 1.625^{1/6} \approx 1.084$: the population grows by about $8.4\%$ a year.
options: This is $b^6$, the growth factor over all six years, not over one year.
Right: the sixth root of $\frac{1{,}950}{1{,}200}$, the growth factor per year.
This splits the $62.5\%$ growth into six equal parts, as if the growth were linear; exponential growth compounds.
This takes a seventh root, counting the seven values $t = 0$ to $6$ instead of the six years between them.

items.q: Let $f(x) = 3 - x$ and $g(x) = \ln(x^2 + 1)$. Find every solution of $f(g(x)) = 1$.
options: $x \approx 2.528$
$x \approx 1.689$ and $x \approx 4.311$
$x \approx -2.528$ and $x \approx 2.528$
$x \approx -2.718$ and $x \approx 2.718$

why.correct: $f(g(x)) = 3 - \ln(x^2 + 1)$. Graph it with $y = 1$ and find both intersections, or solve: $\ln(x^2 + 1) = 2$, so $x^2 + 1 = e^2$ and $x = \pm\sqrt{e^2 - 1} \approx \pm 2.528$.
options: This misses the negative solution; $x^2 + 1$ has the same value at $x$ and $-x$.
This solves $g(f(x)) = 1$: the functions were composed in the other order.
Right: both inputs where $3 - \ln(x^2 + 1) = 1$.
This drops the $+ 1$ and solves $x^2 = e^2$.

items.q: Use a graphing calculator to find every solution of $2^x = 3x + 1$.
options: $x \approx 3.538$
$x = 0$ and $x \approx 3.538$
$x \approx 0.458$ and $x \approx 3.313$

why.correct: Graph $y = 2^x$ and $y = 3x + 1$ and find every intersection. They meet at $x = 0$ (both sides are $1$) and again at $x \approx 3.538$, where the exponential overtakes the line. A window up to $x = 5$ shows both.
options: This misses $x = 0$, where $2^0 = 1 = 3(0) + 1$.
Right: both intersections of $y = 2^x$ and $y = 3x + 1$.
This misses the second intersection; a window that stops near $x = 3$ hides it.
These solve $2^x = 3x$: the $+ 1$ was dropped.

items.q: Monthly sales of a new app are modeled by $S(t) = 12 + 5\ln(t + 1)$ thousand dollars, $t$ months after launch. According to the model, at what time $t$ do monthly sales first reach $25$ thousand dollars?

why.correct: Solve $12 + 5\ln(t + 1) = 25$: $\ln(t + 1) = 2.6$, so $t + 1 = e^{2.6}$ and $t = e^{2.6} - 1 \approx 12.464$ months. Or intersect $y = S(t)$ with $y = 25$ on the calculator.
options: This is $e^{2.6}$, the value of $t + 1$; subtract $1$ to get $t$.
This sets $t + 1 = 2.6$, leaving out the step that undoes the logarithm.
This solves $5\ln(t + 1) = 25$, leaving the $12$ on the left.
Right: the time when $S(t) = 25$.

items.q: The temperature on a summer day is modeled by $T(t) = 58 + 14\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{12}(t - 9)\right)$ degrees Fahrenheit, $t$ hours after midnight, $0 \le t \le 24$. For how many hours of the day is the temperature above $68$ degrees?

why.correct: In radian mode, graph $T$ with $y = 68$. The temperature reaches $68$ at $t \approx 12.039$ and falls back to $68$ at $t \approx 17.961$; it is above $68$ between them, for $17.961 - 12.039 \approx 5.922$ hours. Store both times before subtracting.
options: This is the first time the temperature reaches $68$ degrees, not the length of time above it.
Right: the time between the two crossings of $y = 68$.
This is the number of hours the temperature is at or below $68$ degrees.
This is the second crossing time, when the temperature falls back to $68$ degrees.

items.q: The polar curve $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$ is drawn for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$. Find every $\theta$ in that interval at which $r = 0.4$.
options: $\theta \approx 1.875$
$\theta \approx 1.875$ and $\theta \approx 4.408$
$\theta \approx 1.266$ and $\theta \approx 5.017$
$\theta \approx 107.458$ and $\theta \approx 252.542$

why.correct: Solve $1 + 2\cos\theta = 0.4$: $\cos\theta = -0.3$. In radian mode, $\cos^{-1}(-0.3) \approx 1.875$, and cosine has the same value at $2\pi - 1.875 \approx 4.408$. Both are in $[0, 2\pi)$.
options: This misses the second angle; inverse cosine gives only the one in $[0, \pi]$.
Right: both angles in $[0, 2\pi)$ with $\cos\theta = -0.3$.
These solve $\cos\theta = 0.3$: the sign of $-0.6$ divided by $2$ was lost.
These are in degrees; the calculator was not in radian mode.

items.q: Let $f(x) = x^4 - 5x^2 + 2x + 3$. On which intervals is $f$ decreasing?

why.correct: Graph $f$ and find its three turning points: relative minimums at $x \approx -1.673$ and $x \approx 1.470$, a relative maximum at $x \approx 0.203$. The leading term $x^4$ makes the left end fall from $\infty$, so $f$ is decreasing on $(-\infty, -1.673)$ and $(0.203, 1.470)$. (Either bracket at a turning point is accepted.)
options: These are the intervals where $f$ is increasing.
Right: from the left end down to the first minimum, and from the maximum down to the second minimum.
These are where $f(x) < 0$, below the $x$-axis; being negative is not the same as decreasing.
This finds only the first falling piece; $f$ also falls from its relative maximum at $x \approx 0.203$ to the minimum at $x \approx 1.470$.

items.q: What is the greatest depth of the water for $0 \le t \le 20$?

why.correct: Use the calculator's maximum feature on $w$: the relative maximum is at $t \approx 14.343$, where $w(t) \approx 45.162$ meters. Compare with the ends: $w(0) = 30$ and $w(20) = 30$ are lower, so $45.162$ meters is the greatest depth on the interval.
options: This is the time when the greatest depth occurs, not the depth.
This is the depth at each end of the interval, which is lower than the high point.
Right: the relative maximum value, higher than both endpoint values.
This is the least depth on the interval, at $t \approx 2.324$.

items.q: What is the average rate of change of $w$ on $[4, 12]$, in meters per month?

why.correct: $\frac{w(12) - w(4)}{12 - 4} = \frac{43.44 - 28.72}{8} = 1.840$ meters per month, the slope of the secant line through $(4, w(4))$ and $(12, w(12))$.
options: Right: the change in depth divided by the $8$ months.
This is the change $w(12) - w(4)$, not divided by $12 - 4$.
This subtracts in the wrong order on top: $w(4) - w(12)$.
This is the average of the two depths, not a rate of change.

items.q: Find every time $t$ in $[0, 20]$ at which the depth of the water is $41$ meters.
options: $t \approx 10.515$
$t \approx 10.515$ and $t \approx 17.478$
$t \approx 2.324$ and $t \approx 14.343$
$t \approx 14.343$

why.correct: Graph $w$ with $y = 41$ and find both intersections: $t \approx 10.515$ (rising) and $t \approx 17.478$ (falling). The graph reaches $41$ meters once on the way up and once on the way down.
options: This misses the second time, after the high point, when the depth falls back to $41$ meters.
Right: both times when $w(t) = 41$.
These are the times of the turning points, not of a depth of $41$ meters.
This is the time of the greatest depth, about $45.162$ meters.

items.q: Let $r(x) = \frac{3x^2 - 2}{x^2 - x - 6}$. Use a graphing calculator to find every solution of $r(x) = x$.
options: $x \approx 0.284$ and $x \approx 5.100$
$x \approx -1.383$, $x \approx 0.284$ and $x \approx 5.100$
$x \approx 5.222$

why.correct: Graph $y = r(x)$ and $y = x$ and find every intersection, on each side of the vertical asymptotes $x = -2$ and $x = 3$. (Algebraically, $3x^2 - 2 = x^3 - x^2 - 6x$, so $x^3 - 4x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0$.) The solutions are $x \approx -1.383$, $x \approx 0.284$ and $x \approx 5.100$; none is $-2$ or $3$.
options: This misses the solution between $x = -2$ and $x = 0$; check every piece of the graph between the asymptotes.
These are the vertical asymptotes, where $r$ is undefined, so they cannot be solutions.
Right: all three intersections of $y = r(x)$ and $y = x$.
This solves $x^3 - 4x^2 - 6x - 2 = 0$: a sign slip when $-2$ was moved across.

items.q: The number of members of a club is modeled by $E(t) = 150(1.08)^t$, $t$ months after it started. At $t = 5$ the club had $220$ members. What is the residual of the model at $t = 5$?

why.correct: Residual $=$ actual $-$ predicted $= 220 - 150(1.08)^5 \approx 220 - 220.399 = -0.399$. The model predicts slightly more members than the club had. Keep $1.08^5$ unrounded in the calculator.
options: This is predicted minus actual; a residual is actual minus predicted.
This is the predicted value $E(5)$, not the residual.
This rounds $1.08^5$ to $1.469$ before multiplying; rounding partway changes the third decimal place.
Right: the actual value minus the value the model predicts.

items.q: Let $f(x) = 2 + \ln(x + 3)$ for $x > -3$. What is the value of $f^{-1}(5)$?

why.correct: $f^{-1}(5)$ is the input with $f(x) = 5$: $\ln(x + 3) = 3$, so $x + 3 = e^3$ and $x = e^3 - 3 \approx 17.086$. Check: $f(17.086) \approx 2 + \ln(20.086) \approx 5$.
options: Right: the input that $f$ sends to $5$.
This is $f(5) = 2 + \ln 8$, the output for the input $5$, not the input for the output $5$.
This is $\frac{1}{f(5)}$; the $-1$ in $f^{-1}$ means the inverse function, not the reciprocal.
This solves $\ln(x + 3) = 5$, leaving out the $2$.

items.q: According to the model, how many hours of daylight are there on day $t = 150$?

why.correct: In radian mode, $D(150) = 12.2 + 2.8\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{365}(70)\right) \approx 14.815$ hours.
options: This is the calculator in degree mode; the model is in radians.
Right: the model evaluated at $t = 150$ in radian mode.
This computes $\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{365} \cdot 150 - 80\right)$: the $80$ was subtracted outside the parentheses.
This is the midline value, the daylight on day $80$, not day $150$.

items.q: Find every day $t$ in $[0, 365]$ on which the model gives $14$ hours of daylight.
options: $t \approx 161.122$ and $t \approx 363.878$
$t \approx 120.561$
$t \approx 39.439$ and $t \approx 303.061$
$t \approx 120.561$ and $t \approx 221.939$

why.correct: In radian mode, graph $D$ with $y = 14$ on $0 \le t \le 365$ and find both intersections: $t \approx 120.561$ (daylight growing) and $t \approx 221.939$ (daylight shrinking).
options: These use $b = \frac{\pi}{365}$, a period of $730$ days; the period is $365$ days, so $b = \frac{2\pi}{365}$.
This misses the second day, after the longest day, when the daylight falls back to $14$ hours.
These are the days with $10.4$ hours: the sign of $14 - 12.2$ was flipped.
Right: both days in the interval when $D(t) = 14$.

items.q: What is the average rate of change of $D$ on $[60, 100]$, in hours per day?

why.correct: In radian mode, $\frac{D(100) - D(60)}{100 - 60} \approx \frac{1.890}{40} \approx 0.047$ hours per day, the slope of the secant line through $(60, D(60))$ and $(100, D(100))$. Store $D(100) - D(60)$ before dividing.
options: This is the change $D(100) - D(60)$, not divided by the $40$ days.
This subtracts in the wrong order: $D(60) - D(100)$ over $100 - 60$.
Right: the slope of the secant line on $[60, 100]$.
This is the calculator in degree mode; in radians the change is much larger.

items.q: Use a graphing calculator in radian mode to find every solution of $3\sin(2x) = 1 + x$ on $[0, \pi]$.
options: $x \approx 0.207$
$x \approx 0.538$ and $x \approx 1.868$
There is no solution in $[0, \pi]$
$x \approx 0.207$ and $x \approx 1.167$

why.correct: Graph $y = 3\sin(2x)$ and $y = 1 + x$ on $0 \le x \le \pi$ in radian mode. The line crosses the first hump of the sine curve twice: $x \approx 0.207$ and $x \approx 1.167$. After that the sine curve is below the line.
options: This misses the second crossing, where the sine curve falls back below the line.
These solve $3\sin x = 1 + x$: the $2$ inside the sine was dropped.
This is what degree mode shows; in radians the curves cross twice.
Right: both intersections in $[0, \pi]$.
